reliefs.cap_rule: Per qualifying person: the lesser of Schedule 1 page 2 line 15 (line 5, the lesser of total earned income and the 5,000 maximum earned income, plus line 14, interest, dividends, alimony, capital gains, other income, taxable IRA distributions, taxable pensions and rental/royalty/partnership/S corp income, zero if less) and line 16, the maximum allowable exclusion. The 5,000 earned-income limit is one combined limit on salary and wages plus other earned income (lines 1-5), recorded as a sub_limit on each. Income from jointly owned property is allocated 50% to each spouse. Part-year residents and nonresidents prorate the earned and unearned portions separately.

notes: Settlement 2026-11-07: reliefs retirement exclusion (all three age branches) covers wages and self_employment: A said sub_limits only (not in covers), B said in covers with the sub_limits; booklet PDF page 48 Schedule 1 page 2 lines 1-5 take 'Salary and wages' and 'Other Earned Income' up to 'Maximum Earned Income' 5,000, and PDF page 31 says 'only $5,000 of the wages can be included in the RIE'. B followed.

Settlement 2026-11-07: reliefs retirement exclusion covers employer_plan_distribution: A said covers, B said covers_unclear; PDF page 48 lines 11-12 name only 'Taxable IRA Distributions' and 'Taxable Pensions', and no page names 401(k), 403(b), 457 or employer plans. B followed at settlement; settled into covers the same day by the maintainer decision (next note).

Maintainer decision 2026-11-07 (docs/decisions.md): employer_plan_distribution (401(k), 403(b), 457) and roth_conversion moved from covers_unclear to covers in all three retirement exclusion entries (62-64, disabled under 62, 65 or older). Sources, 2025 IT-511 booklet: the worksheet takes every kind of unearned income in Georgia income: Schedule 1 page 2 lines 6-13 'Interest Income', 'Dividend Income', 'Alimony', 'Capital Gains (Losses)', 'Other Income (Losses)', 'Taxable IRA Distributions', 'Taxable Pensions', 'Rental, Royalty, Partnership, S Corp, etc.' (PDF page 48; 2025GA500.pdf page 8; the same lines in the PDF page 24 example); PDF page 24 leaves out only 'Social Security and Railroad Retirement paid by the Railroad Retirement Board, exempt interest, or other income that is not taxable to Georgia' and income 'from lotteries, gambling, illegal sources, or similar income'. Georgia starts from federal AGI (PDF page 16 Line 8), so a taxable 401(k), 403(b) or 457 payout is Georgia income and lands on the 'Taxable Pensions' line (or 'Other Income'); it is not among the kinds left out. PDF page 12: 'The provisions concerning taxability and conversion from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA are the same for Georgia and the Internal Revenue Service', so the taxable part of a conversion is a taxable IRA distribution, line 11. The DOR Retirees FAQ (retirees-faq.page.txt) says retirement income includes 'interest, dividends, net rentals, capital gains, royalties, pensions, annuities'. Georgia rule 560-7-4-.02 says 'income from pensions and annuities, and other similar income' and agrees, but it is not archived (rules.sos.ga.gov refuses automated download), so it is not cited as a source here.

Settlement 2026-11-07: reliefs retirement exclusion public_pension_other_state: A said not listed (falls under the generic taxable pensions line), B said covers_unclear; PDF page 48 line 12 'Taxable Pensions' has no limit by payer, PDF page 13 says 'Full-year residents are taxed on all income, except tax-exempt income, regardless of the source or where derived', and PDF page 24 removes only income 'not taxable to Georgia'. Moved to covers (rule 15a: same entry as Georgia's own public pensions).
Settlement 2026-11-07: reliefs ga_social_security_railroad (A only): kept; PDF page 22 Subtractions item 5 prints it and it is Social Security relief, in scope.
Settlement 2026-11-07: reliefs ga_us_obligations_interest (A only): kept; PDF page 22 Subtractions item 4 prints it (kept for South Carolina too).

Rate: one flat rate of 5.19% for every filing status (What's New PDF page 9; Line 16 PDF page 17; Form 500 line 16). The booklet prints no bracket schedule and no tax table; recorded as one bracket from 0. No surtax and no recapture found in the booklet.
Georgia starts from federal AGI (Line 8: 'Do not use Federal taxable income').

Deductions: the standard deduction (24,000 joint; 12,000 single, separate, head of household, qualifying surviving spouse) and a 4,000 dependent exemption. The booklet prints no personal or spouse exemption and no age-65 or blind amount (not found in the booklet).

Social Security: exempt. Subtractions item 5 (PDF page 22) and Schedule 1 line 8 subtract the taxable portion; the DOR Retirees FAQ says 'Taxable Social Security and Railroad Retirement on the Federal return are exempt from Georgia Income Tax.'

Pensions: the booklet does not split government from private pensions. Schedule 1 page 2 line 12 is one 'Taxable Pensions' line, so public_pension, public_pension_other_state and private_pension share the same entries. No rule specific to another state's government pension (New York State included) is found in the booklet; such a pension is a taxable pension like any other.

Georgia's own and federal government pensions: no exemption of their own; they fall under the retirement exclusion. The only Georgia-specific pension rule is Subtractions item 12 (PDF page 22): an adjustment for teachers retired from the Teacher's Retirement System of Georgia for contributions paid between July 1, 1987, and December 31, 1989, that were reported to and taxed by Georgia. It recovers previously taxed contributions, not pension income, so it is not recorded as a relief (an uncapped entry covering public_pension would read as a full exemption). No contributory-plan test is printed.

Roth conversions: PDF page 12 says 'The provisions concerning taxability and conversion from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA are the same for Georgia and the Internal Revenue Service.' The taxable part of a conversion is therefore a taxable IRA distribution on Schedule 1 page 2 line 11, and it is in covers (maintainer decision 2026-11-07, note above).

Military retirement: its own exclusion for those under 62 (17,500, plus another 17,500 with more than 17,500 of Georgia earned income; Schedule 1 page 3 line 7 prints 35,000). Whether military retirement counts as 'Taxable Pensions' in the retirement exclusion at 62 or older is not stated (covers_unclear). Whether an under-62 disabled filer may take both the military and the disability exclusion is not stated.

Earned income in the retirement exclusion: the booklet and form print 5,000 (PDF page 21, page 24 example, Schedule 1 page 2 line 4). The DOR Retirees FAQ says 'the first $4000.00 of earned income'; this conflicts with the booklet and is not used.
Retirement exclusion branches: each spouse qualifies separately (PDF page 21). The age branches are exclusive, so no best_of_group. No income test is printed.
Additions item 3 (PDF page 20): lump sum distributions from employee benefit plans reported on IRS Form 4972 are added; no field holds this.
Subtractions item 7 (PDF page 22): IRA, Keogh and SEP withdrawals on which Georgia tax was paid because of 1981-1986 differences are subtracted; not recorded as a relief (historical basis).

Out of scope and not recorded as reliefs: the Low Income Credit (federal AGI less than 20,000; PDF pages 17 and 35), the Georgia Eligible Itemizer Tax Credit (up to 300 per taxpayer; PDF page 9), the credit for taxes paid to other states (PDF page 34), Path2College 529 contributions (Subtractions item 15).
Capital gains: no rate or deduction different from ordinary income is printed; capital gains are, however, income the retirement exclusion may be applied to.
Indexing: the booklet says nothing about inflation adjustment of any figure.
Part-year residents and nonresidents prorate the retirement exclusion (PDF page 24); not recorded further.
